recommender_rubric.justification:
Feasibility (4): The opening package (aggregated_by_district maps, joint_asean_panel, partial_exemptions, partial_donor_fund) matches what Indonesia has signaled. It fits the Article 27 consultation framework and the Presidential Regulation 1/2016 BRG channel. Tranche-based funding tied to verified results is workable. Gaps: it never says who verifies hotspot reductions, and it doesn't say how a panel with no treaty basis would be set up.

Tradeoff coverage (3): It names the main tensions. These are attribution against sovereignty, funding against verified results, and the untested Act against the diplomatic cost. The first option's risk flags that district maps may not prove ownership under Section 8. It does not address the smallholder-versus-corporate distinction, the land-tenure overlaps, the agribusiness lobby's effect on the deal, or the planting-window timing. The moratorium issue is covered only through the funding option.

Priority consistency (3): Results-linked funding respects Singapore's red line on funding without measurable reductions. The attribution red line is at risk. The headline concedes the Act as the main route and accepts district maps that the recommendation itself admits may not support Section 8 attribution. The panel's attribution standard is left undefined, so it is unclear that an attribution mechanism survives. The rationale says "Singapore bears" the costs, and the funding language suggests Singapore would pay. That sits uneasily with the stated aim of holding corporate actors accountable. Corporate accountability is mostly deferred to a fallback option.

Counterpart consideration (4): It engages Indonesia's data-law constraint, its objection to foreign courts, and its smallholder funding need. It offers a joint panel and a partial fund. It never mentions Indonesia's fiscal limits beyond the risk that Indonesia asks for more, and it doesn't engage with the tenure disputes.

Strong arguments (3): It uses the lack of a tribunal in the 2002 agreement and the Section 8 map-based presumption. It also uses the untested extraterritorial reach and the fact that Singapore cannot compel enforcement. It misses Article 8(1) data-sharing obligations as leverage and the Article 3(1) duty not to cause damage. It also misses the Section 6 private suit as a lever, which the first option mentions only in passing. The rationale partly contradicts itself: it blames Indonesian operators and parents, then proposes a deal that softens liability for them.

Options: 3 options. All three are distinct. They are conditional branches covering maps/enforcement, funding, and a walk-away fallback. There are no alternative offers within a branch, and the moratorium issue has no dedicated option.

transcript.position: Singapore opens with a package built on attribution, because without it the haze will return every dry season. In 2015 our 24-hour PSI passed 300 and schools closed, and regional losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars, yet the 2002 ASEAN Agreement gives no court or tribunal and only amicable consultation, so nobody was held to account. We therefore ask Indonesia to share full concession maps with the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, so that fires can be tied to the companies that hold the land, and we ask for a joint ASEAN panel to hear attribution cases, which respects Indonesian sovereignty while giving the region a forum the treaty lacks. We also ask for a peatland moratorium with no exemptions for existing concessions, because most of the burning sits on drained peat. In return, Singapore will direct a partial donor fund for restoration, released in tranches only against measured reductions in hotspots and PSI days. The most damaging objection is that sharing maps infringes Indonesian sovereignty and domestic data law. Our answer is that the 2002 Agreement itself obliges parties to exchange fire and haze data, that the maps would sit inside a regional body and not be handed to Singapore's courts, and that the panel route means we do not need to apply our own Act inside Indonesia. If Indonesia accepts the maps and the panel, Singapore can hold its own Act in reserve and accept a funded, phased approach on the moratorium. We will not accept any settlement without an attribution mechanism, and we will not pay for transition without measurable reductions, because an unconditional fund would pay for the same burning that causes our hazardous days.

transcript.position: Indonesia accepts that the 2015 haze, with Singapore's 24-hour PSI above 300 between June and October, was a real harm and that it must be prevented. However, the cure has to run through Indonesian law and Indonesian courts, because enforcement on our soil belongs to our own authorities. The ASEAN Agreement already balances the two duties: Article 3(1) keeps each party's sovereign right to use its resources alongside a duty not to harm neighbours, and Article 9 obliges us to control open burning. Singapore's Act reaches conduct outside Singapore under section 4 and presumes liability from land ownership under section 8, using maps supplied by a foreign government. That would make our concession registry, which overlaps unresolved tenure disputes, the evidence in a foreign court. We therefore propose that Indonesian courts and the Peatland Restoration Agency, set up in January 2016, handle enforcement. The most serious objection is that Article 27 offers no tribunal, so Indonesian enforcement may look unaccountable. We answer it with data. We will give aggregated district-level fire and concession data through the ASEAN channel that Article 8(1) already provides, which lets Singapore and the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System see where fires burn without disclosing parcel-level maps that our data law restricts. In return, a phased moratorium with partial exemptions protects smallholders through the planting window, and a donor fund must pay for the transition. Indonesia cannot carry the cost alone, and no restriction can fall on smallholders without funded alternatives. We will move on the moratorium and on district-level data only if donors commit to a full transition fund and Singapore drops its jurisdiction claim.

Singapore opens with a package built on one need: a way to say who is responsible for a fire that survives beyond this episode. Singapore's 24-hour PSI passed 300 in 2015, schools closed, and regional losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars [Background]. Because the 2002 ASEAN agreement has no court or tribunal and settles disputes only by consultation [S1 Article 27], good data is the only enforcement tool the region has. We therefore ask Indonesia to give full concession maps to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, which Article 8(1) already envisions as a flow of fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre [S1]. In return we drop our demand that Singapore's own law be the forum for cases, and accept a joint ASEAN panel to hear attribution and corporate liability cases. This answers Indonesia's sovereignty objection, because Indonesian officials would sit on the body that uses the maps and no Singapore court would act inside Indonesian territory.

The most damaging objection is that Singapore is trying to prosecute Indonesian firms abroad. The Act is narrower than that: the aggregate fine is capped at S$2 million [S2 section 5(5)], so it is a lever for evidence rather than a revenue threat. The real value lies in the presumption that a landowner where a fire burns caused the haze, which can be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government [S2 section 8], so the maps and the panel replace the need for unilateral action. We also ask for a peatland moratorium with no exemptions for existing concessions, because exemptions let burning continue on the land where it recurs every dry season. In return, Singapore will direct regional development and donor funding to a partial transition fund, but only against measured reductions in hotspots and PSI days. We will not accept any deal without an attribution mechanism, and we will not pay into a fund with no measurable reductions, because that would spend public money while the cycle continues.

However, the cure must work on Indonesian soil under Indonesian authority. scores.justification: A joint ASEAN panel is a new body. The cited treaty has no tribunal [S1 Art. 27], and Singapore gives no design for it, such as membership, powers, or how it would bind companies. Full concession maps also run into Indonesia's stated sovereignty and data-law objections. The funding link to measured reductions is workable in principle but is not built out.

It cites exact legal figures (S$2 million cap, s.8 presumption) and gives a clear package. The partial fund has no size, no hotspot or PSI-day thresholds and no payment schedule. The panel has no procedure.

Singapore admits it gives up its own Act as the main forum. It mostly says the costs to Indonesia are small ('costs Indonesia little', 'a lever for evidence rather than a revenue threat'). It does not admit that releasing maps still exposes concession holders to the s.8 presumption and s.6 civil suits, or that Indonesia bears the cost of the moratorium with no exemptions.

judgments.summary: Singapore proposes that Indonesia hand over full concession maps to the regional haze monitoring system. In exchange, Singapore would drop its own law as the main forum and accept a joint ASEAN panel to decide who is responsible for fires and corporate liability. It also asks for a peatland moratorium with no exemptions and offers a partial donor fund paid only against measured falls in hotspots and bad-air days. The case is clear and well tied to the treaty and the Act. It is thin on how the panel would work and on the size of the fund, and it understates what the maps would expose Indonesian firms to.

It is vague on how domestic enforcement would deliver accountability, and some of its support (El Nino odds, tenure disputes) is not backed by the listed sources.

It cites the S$2 million cap, S$100,000 per day, tranches against hotspots and PSI days, referral to the panel before the Act, and smallholders first. It gives no tranche sizes, no hotspot or PSI targets, no panel composition or voting rules, and no verification timeline.

It admits that Indonesia's domestic data law may need time and that overlapping tenure could pin liability on the wrong party, and it adds a verification step. It opens by stating it has moved on the moratorium (none to partial exemptions) and on funding (partial to full), and it explains these as responses to Indonesia's priorities. recommender_rubric.justification:
Three conditional fallback options are given, and they cover different branches: panel rejection, a full-funding demand, and a no-panel moratorium offer. All three are distinct, though they touch overlapping issues.

Priority consistency is good (4). The options keep Singapore's two red lines: an attribution mechanism and funding only against measured results. The third option openly flags the risk of hollowing out attribution. The opening package matches Singapore's round-3 position, except that it asks for a full moratorium with no exemptions. That is a harder opening than Singapore's own round-3 move to partial exemptions, though it is defensible as an ask. The rationale says the deal holds "under any priority", which is unsupported.

Feasibility is middling (3). Option 1 offers an attribution-only panel to a party whose stated red line is no panel with power over conduct on its soil. Indonesia said it cannot move if Singapore insists on a panel. The option's own risk note admits Indonesia may refuse, and the panel design is unspecified. Option 3 is hard to execute: it requires an attribution record "outside Indonesian courts", and Indonesia has rejected that. Option 2 holds at a partial fund while Indonesia demands a full fund in writing up front. It has no mechanism to bridge that gap, such as a written commitment from donors or a staged pool. The option also says Singapore "accepts... weather-adjusted tranches", but that was already Singapore's position, so it is not a concession.

Tradeoff coverage is partial (3). The recommendation covers the panel versus sovereignty, funding conditionality versus smallholder timing, and attribution versus enforcement independence. It does not address the uncapped section 6 civil liability, which Singapore refused to trade away and Indonesia contested. Option 1's risk note mentions it only briefly. It also does not address the tenure-overlap and verification issue in any depth, or Singapore's domestic agribusiness lobby.

Counterpart consideration is adequate (3). It meets several Indonesian concerns: smallholders get first call on the money, district-level data protects the parcel registry, no section 8 use is promised, and the ministry runs parcel verification. But the rationale says Indonesia "should bear enforcement cost", which pays little attention to Indonesia's fiscal constraint. Option 2 pushes back on Indonesia's funding ask without offering a solution.

Strong arguments are moderately reflected (3). The recommendation draws on the section 8 and district-data point, the rainfall-adjusted tranches, and the Article 27 no-tribunal gap behind the attribution red line. It does not use the stronger rebuttal that Singapore's Act stays in force whichever forum is chosen, which was Indonesia's best point. Nor does it use the argument that section 8 depends on owner identification, which district data does not provide.

transcript.position:
Singapore opens with a package built on one need: an attribution mechanism that still works after this episode ends. The 2015 fires pushed our 24-hour PSI past 300 between June and October and cost the region tens of billions of dollars, and without data on who holds each concession, nobody can show which company's land burned, so the cycle repeats every dry season. We therefore ask Indonesia to give its plantation concession maps in full to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System. This is not a threat to sovereignty, because Article 3(1) of the ASEAN Agreement keeps each state's right to exploit its resources alongside a duty not to damage its neighbours, and Article 8(1) already obliges each party's monitoring centre to pass fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre. Maps are the missing piece of a duty Indonesia has already accepted.

In return, Singapore will move on enforcement. We would accept a joint ASEAN panel rather than applying our own Act, because that answers Indonesia's objection to extraterritorial reach, and our Act's S$2 million aggregate cap on fines is modest next to the damage. The panel fills a real gap, since Article 27 offers only consultation and no tribunal. We also ask for a full peatland moratorium with no exemptions, since exempting existing concessions leaves the burning land untouched. Singapore will help pay for transition through a partial donor fund, but only if payments are tied to measurable reductions in hotspots and haze days. We cannot compel enforcement inside Indonesia, and we will not pay for promises. If Indonesia refuses any attribution mechanism, we will fall back on applying our Act, which is our leverage and not our preference.

key_claims.claim: Full concession maps are needed because attribution depends on knowing who owns burning land, and the 2015 haze pushed Singapore's PSI above 300 for a season.
key_claims.evidence: Section 8 of the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act 2014 presumes the owner or occupier of land where a fire burns caused the haze and allows ownership to be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government [S2], and the scenario records PSI above 300 between June and October 2015 [Background].

key_claims.claim: Sharing maps with the monitoring system is consistent with Indonesia's sovereignty because it extends a data duty Indonesia already accepted.
key_claims.evidence: Article 8(1) requires each party's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and Article 3(1) pairs the sovereign right to exploit resources with a duty not to damage other states [S1].

key_claims.claim: A joint ASEAN panel is a real concession from Singapore and fills a gap in the regional framework.
key_claims.evidence: Article 27 of the ASEAN Agreement leaves disputes to consultation or negotiation with no court or tribunal [S1], while our own Act reaches conduct outside Singapore under section 4 and carries fines of up to S$100,000 per day, capped at S$2 million in aggregate [S2].

key_claims.claim: Transition funding must be conditional on results because the scale of the 2015 losses shows that unconditioned money would not be justified.
key_claims.evidence: Regional economic losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars in the 2015 episode [Background]; Singapore therefore offers a partial fund tied to measurable reductions in hotspots and haze days, and the baseline figures would need to be agreed with Indonesia's Peatland Restoration Agency, established in January 2016 [Background].

concessions: Singapore will accept a joint ASEAN panel instead of applying its Act to Indonesian-based companies, if Indonesia releases full concession maps.
Singapore will contribute to a partial donor fund rather than seeking a full one, if payments are tied to measurable reductions.
red_lines: No settlement without an attribution mechanism: without it the 2015 episode, with PSI above 300, can recur with no responsible party identified.
No transition funding without measurable reductions: unconditioned money would repeat the pattern behind tens of billions of dollars in regional losses.

transcript.position:
Indonesia takes the 2015 haze seriously and is ready to act, but it will act through its own courts and agencies, with the transition paid for. The regional treaty we all signed already gives us the framework: Article 3(1) of the ASEAN haze agreement keeps each party's sovereign right to use its resources alongside a duty not to harm neighbours, and Article 27 says disputes are settled by consultation, with no court or tribunal. Singapore's Act reaches conduct abroad (section 4) and presumes that a landowner caused any haze (section 8), so applying it would set up a foreign court ruling on acts on Indonesian soil. We cannot accept that, so we ask that enforcement stay with Indonesian courts, with the Peatland Restoration Agency and provincial administrations carrying out the moratorium. In return, we offer a moratorium with limited exemptions for existing smallholder plots, and concession data shared as district-level aggregates with the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System. That gives Singapore and ASEAN the fire-risk picture that Article 8(1) is meant to deliver, without parcel-level disclosure that our data law restricts and that overlaps unresolved tenure disputes.

The most damaging objection to this is that Indonesia is asking for sovereignty and money while the PSI passed 300 in Singapore, so we are shielding the companies that caused the fires. We answer that district-level data still shows where fires and clearing cluster, and our own courts can prosecute the companies. The Singapore Act's fines are capped at S$2 million in total (section 5(5)), so its deterrent is small next to a funded restoration programme. A restriction that lands on smallholders without alternatives would simply push them back to burning during the planting window, with El Nino conditions more than 90% likely to last through the northern winter. Therefore a donor fund is the cheapest way to cut haze, not a favour to Indonesia. Indonesia cannot carry that transition alone, so we ask for a fully funded donor transition fund. If donors and Singapore accept Indonesian-court enforcement and the funding, we can move on the moratorium exemptions and on the level of data detail.

key_claims.claim: A foreign statute applied to Indonesian soil would create a foreign-court precedent that the regional treaty deliberately avoids, and the treaty already provides a route through consultation.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 says disputes are settled amicably by consultation or negotiation with no court or tribunal, and [S2] section 4 extends the Singapore Act to conduct outside Singapore, so applying it would go beyond the dispute process all parties signed in 2002.

key_claims.claim: Singapore's penalty regime is a weak deterrent next to a funded restoration and transition programme, so Indonesian enforcement plus funding serves Singapore's clean-air interest better.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(5) caps the aggregate fine at S$2 million, even though section 5(2)(a) allows up to S$100,000 per day, while the 2015 episode pushed the PSI past 300 and caused regional losses in the tens of billions of dollars [Background].

key_claims.claim: Sharing district-level aggregated data meets the treaty's data-sharing purpose without breaching Indonesian data law or exposing unresolved tenure disputes.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) requires fire and haze data to go to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, which aggregated data can satisfy, while [S2] section 8 would let maps supplied by a foreign government decide who is presumed to have caused a fire, which is risky where the concession registry overlaps tenure disputes [Background].

key_claims.claim: The transition needs donor funding now because the fire risk is highest in the coming dry season and the planting window is short.
key_claims.evidence: El Nino conditions are under way with a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter [Background, ENSO Diagnostic Discussion, 13 August 2015], and [S1] Article 9 obliges parties to prevent land clearing by fire, which smallholders cannot do without an affordable alternative.

concessions: Indonesia will accept a moratorium with only partial exemptions, if donors fund the transition and enforcement stays with Indonesian courts.
Indonesia will share district-level aggregated concession data with the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, if parcel-level data stays under domestic control.
red_lines: No foreign jurisdiction over acts on Indonesian soil: applying the Singapore Act in Indonesia would put Indonesian companies and officials before a foreign court, which we cannot accept.
No restriction that falls on smallholders without funded alternatives: a moratorium without funding would remove smallholders' income during the planting window and push them back to burning.

scores.justification: A joint panel and a results-tied partial fund are workable ideas, but the full maps demand collides with Indonesia's stated data-law limits. Singapore also admits it 'cannot compel enforcement inside Indonesia', and no panel design or funding size is given.

It names exact options and cites the S$2 million cap. The fund has no amount or donor split, and 'measurable reductions in hotspots and haze days' has no thresholds. Baselines are left to be agreed with the Peatland Restoration Agency.

It admits that dropping its Act and accepting a panel is a concession, and that it will not pay for promises. It says little about what full maps and a moratorium with no exemptions cost Indonesia: sovereignty concerns, smallholder livelihoods and tenure disputes.
Round 1. The package, concessions and red lines match its opening statement, including the fallback to applying its Act if no attribution mechanism is agreed.
Round 1 with no prior opponent argument. It anticipates Indonesia's objection to extraterritorial reach and its sovereignty argument, but does not address smallholders or the data-law restriction.

judgments.summary: Singapore asks for full concession maps to be given to the regional haze monitoring system and for a moratorium with no exemptions. In return it would accept a joint regional panel instead of applying its own Act, and it would contribute to a partial donor fund tied to measured falls in hotspots and haze days. It says it will fall back on its Act if no attribution mechanism is agreed. The argument is coherent and well grounded in the treaty, but it is thin on figures. It says little about the costs to Indonesia and smallholders.
unsupported_claims: Section 8 'allows ownership to be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government' is supported, but the claim that Article 8(1) is 'the missing piece' that obliges map sharing is an inference: Article 8(1) covers fire and haze data, not concession maps.
'PSI above 300 for a season': the scenario says the 24-hour PSI passed 300 at some point in June to October, not for the whole season.

scores.justification: Enforcement through its own courts, with the Peatland Restoration Agency and provincial administrations running the moratorium, uses existing institutions. District-level data sharing is workable. A fully funded donor transition depends on donors it has not secured.
It specifies the exemption scope (existing smallholder plots), the data level (district aggregates) and the El Nino window. It gives no fund size, no timeline and no prosecution commitments.

It states the 'most damaging objection' that it is shielding companies, and answers it. It does not concede that aggregate data weakens attribution, or that its own courts may be less credible on enforcement.
Round 1. The package matches its opening position. The conditional moves on exemptions and data detail are framed as trades for enforcement and funding.

It engages Singapore's Act directly (sections 4, 5(5), 8) and its attribution rationale. It argues that Article 8(1) can be met with aggregates and turns the S$2 million cap into an argument. It does not directly answer the claim that data is needed to identify who is responsible.

judgments.summary: Indonesia asks that enforcement stay with its own courts, with a moratorium that exempts existing smallholder plots and district-level concession data shared with the regional monitoring system. It also asks for a fully funded donor transition. It argues that funding smallholders is the cheapest way to cut haze and that Singapore's fines are a weak deterrent. transcript.position:
Singapore opens with a package built on attribution, because without knowing who owns the land where fires burn, no cycle of dry-season haze can be broken. Our 24-hour PSI passed 300 in the 2015 episode and regional losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars [Background], so we ask Indonesia to give full concession maps to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, to accept a joint ASEAN panel for enforcement, and to apply its new peatland moratorium with no exemptions. In return, Singapore will direct a partial donor fund for restoration, released in tranches only as measured reductions in hotspots are verified by satellite. We will not fund transition without measurable reductions, and we will not sign a settlement with no attribution mechanism, because paying for restoration that nobody can audit would repeat the 2015 loss.

We expect Indonesia's strongest objection to be sovereignty. We answer that the maps would go to a regional body under the data-sharing duty each party already carries, and that Indonesia keeps its sovereign right to exploit its resources under the 2002 treaty, subject to the duty not to damage neighbours [S1]. A joint panel, rather than applying Singapore's Act on Indonesian land, is itself our concession to that concern, and we offer it on condition that the maps are shared. Our Act, by contrast, caps total fines at S$2 million, so it is a tool for attribution and not an economic threat to Indonesian companies [S2]. Because the 2002 treaty offers only consultation and no tribunal, a panel is the only route that gives attribution a lasting home beyond this episode [S1]. We know we cannot compel enforcement inside Indonesia, so we are offering money and monitoring, not coercion, and we are open to discussing the pace of fund tranches and the panel's composition.

key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 8: an entity owning or occupying land where a fire burns is presumed to have caused the haze, and ownership can be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government.

key_claims.claim: Our legal tool is modest in money terms, so Indonesia's fear of punitive extraterritorial reach is overstated: fines run at S$100,000 per day but total no more than S$2 million.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(2)(a) sets up to S$100,000 per day and section 5(5) caps the aggregate fine at S$2 million, against regional losses in the tens of billions of dollars [Background].

key_claims.claim: A joint panel fills a real gap, because the 2002 regional treaty has no court or tribunal and settles disputes only by consultation, which failed to prevent the 2015 episode.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27: disputes are settled amicably by consultation or negotiation; there is no court or tribunal. The PSI passed 300 in 2015 [Background].

key_claims.claim: Sharing the maps is consistent with duties Indonesia already accepted, so it is not a new sovereignty surrender.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) requires each party's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and Article 9 requires parties to prevent land clearing using fire.

transcript.position:
Indonesia accepts that the 2015 haze, with Singapore's 24-hour PSI passing 300, was a real regional harm, and we are ready to act on it. However, the remedy must be built on Indonesian authority, because the 2002 ASEAN haze agreement confirms each party's sovereign right over its own resources and sets no court or tribunal, only consultation (Articles 3(1) and 27). Singapore's 2014 Act reaches conduct outside Singapore (section 4) and presumes a landowner caused the haze, using maps supplied by a foreign government (section 8). That would turn our concession maps into evidence for foreign civil suits. Therefore Indonesia proposes that enforcement stays with Indonesian courts and the Ministry of Environment and Forestry, and that parcel-level concession maps are withheld, since domestic data law restricts disclosure and land-tenure disputes still overlap the registry. Sharing flawed maps would expose the wrong people to liability.

In return, Indonesia offers a real moratorium: provincial administrations implement a phased peatland moratorium with partial exemptions, and the planned Peatland Restoration Agency will restore degraded land. With El Nino conditions more than 90% likely to last through the 2015-16 northern winter, this is urgent. However, a ban that falls on smallholders without alternatives would simply push them back to burning, and Indonesia cannot fund the transition alone. We therefore ask for a full donor fund for transition costs. If donors commit to it, we can discuss further steps on moratorium scope and on district-level aggregated fire and haze data under Article 8(1). The objection we expect is that withholding maps blocks accountability. Our answer is that Indonesian courts can act against burners on our own soil, and the Act's S$2 million aggregate cap (section 5(5)) is tiny against regional losses in the tens of billions of dollars, so it is no real deterrent. Funded prevention is a better one.

key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 says disputes are settled amicably by consultation or negotiation, with no court or tribunal, and Article 3(1) keeps each party's sovereign right to exploit its own resources, so enforcement on Indonesian soil belongs to Indonesian courts.

key_claims.evidence: [S2] Section 4 extends the Act to conduct outside Singapore, and section 8 presumes an owner or occupier of burning land caused the haze, provable from maps supplied by a foreign government, which makes our registry a litigation tool.

key_claims.evidence: [S2] Section 5(5) caps the aggregate fine at S$2 million, while the scenario [Background] puts regional economic losses in the tens of billions of dollars.

key_claims.evidence: [Background] El Nino conditions are under way with a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter (ENSO Diagnostic Discussion, 13 August 2015).

key_claims.claim: Indonesia already meets its treaty duty on fire control and data reporting through its own channels, so it needs no foreign mechanism.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 9 requires parties to control open burning, and Article 8(1) requires each party's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, which Indonesia can do without releasing parcel-level maps.

Second, no entity is named until a 60-day correction window has let Indonesia's Ministry of Environment and Forestry fix overlapping tenure claims, which meets Indonesia's fear of exposing the wrong people. unsupported_claims: The claim that the 2015 PSI above 300 'shows what unaudited prevention failed to stop' is not supported: nothing in the sources says prevention was unaudited or that audits were absent in 2015.

scores.justification: District-level hotspot reporting by the Ministry of Environment and Forestry and the use of existing Indonesian courts are within Indonesia's current capacity. The fallback of phasing the smallholder moratorium to match funding is practical. It depends on donors committing a full fund, which Indonesia does not control.

It makes clear commitments: all peatland covered through provincial administrations, district hotspot counts per district, tranche release against verified reductions, an interim dry-season arrangement and a registry that separates smallholders from companies. It gives no fund amount, no timeline and no courts' procedure.

It says that dropping exemptions 'costs us little in the way of leverage', which understates the cost. It does not say that withholding parcel maps limits Singapore's ability to attribute fires. It does acknowledge that a full ban hits farmers in the planting window.

It states its moves: it drops partial exemptions and offers district data and tranche-based release. The red lines on foreign jurisdiction and on unfunded smallholder restrictions are unchanged. One small shift is that the red line now names 'a joint panel with enforcement power'. This is a narrowing of its earlier stance, but it is not explained.

It engages Singapore's modest-fines argument directly by pointing to uncapped section 6 suits. It does not address Singapore's new safeguards (the 60-day correction window, the pledge not to use maps under the Act, the panel's role) and instead argues against a panel with enforcement power, which Singapore did not propose.

judgments.summary: Indonesia accepts a moratorium without exemptions and offers district-level hotspot data and tranche-based fund release. It insists on a full donor fund, enforcement through Indonesian courts and no parcel maps. It argues that parcel maps would feed uncapped private suits in Singapore. It proposes an interim dry-season arrangement and a registry that separates smallholders from companies. The concessions are clear and in line with its earlier position. It largely does not engage with Singapore's safeguards, and the claim that a joint panel adds no power is open to challenge.
unsupported_claims: The claim that a joint panel's findings 'could not be enforced on Indonesian soil' is an inference from S1 Article 27 and Article 3(1), neither of which addresses a new joint panel agreed in this deal.

The claim that Indonesian courts 'will act against the responsible concession holder' once a fire is traced to a district is not supported by any source, and district-level data does not identify a holder.
The claim that a full ban without funding would repeat a PSI above 300 is a speculative extension of the 2015 background.
The statement that the registry overlaps unresolved tenure claims is carried over from the scenario's description of land-tenure disputes and is not supported by the listed sources.

unaddressed_tradeoffs: Section 6 private suits in Singapore are not blocked by Singapore's undertaking not to use the maps under the Act. Neither side says how a government pledge could stop private plaintiffs from using the maps once they are shared.
Neither side says who pays for a full donor fund if donors do not come forward, or what happens to smallholders if tranches shrink or are held back while verification is disputed.
Neither side addresses the cost to Singapore of paying a full fund with weak attribution, or the fiscal cost to Indonesia of enforcing a ban on all peatland.
Neither side says how a verified hotspot reduction would be credited to a district, a concession holder or a smallholder, so tranche triggers could be gamed or disputed.
Neither side says how overlapping tenure claims would be settled if the 60-day correction window is too short, or who decides disputed ownership.
Neither side says what Indonesia's refusal of parcel maps would mean for the regional treaty duties on data sharing in later years or for precedent among other ASEAN states.

transcript.position: Singapore asks for a settlement that ends the yearly haze cycle by making it possible to prove who burned what. In 2015 our 24-hour PSI passed 300, schools closed and regional losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars [Background]. The 2002 ASEAN Agreement already requires each party to control open burning (Article 9) and to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre (Article 8(1)), but it has no court or tribunal and settles disputes only by consultation (Article 27). Therefore nothing in it can say who is responsible. We will not sign a deal with no attribution mechanism, because without one the next dry season repeats this one. Our package is this: Indonesia gives full concession maps to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, and a joint ASEAN panel reviews attribution and enforcement cases, so Indonesia keeps the process regional and our Act is not applied directly. We also ask for a full peatland moratorium with no exemptions, and a partial donor fund for transition, released only against measured reductions in hotspots and PSI days. The most damaging objection is sovereignty: Indonesia says sharing maps breaches its rights. However, Article 3(1) of the Agreement itself pairs the sovereign right to use resources with a duty not to damage other states, so sharing maps with a regional body is the means of meeting that duty and not a surrender of it. In return for the maps and the moratorium, we give up direct application of our Act, which is a real concession because our Act reaches conduct abroad (section 4) and allows fines of up to S$100,000 per day (section 5(2)(a)). We also offer to direct donor money to Indonesian restoration work, but only if reductions are measurable, because we cannot fund transition on trust. Singapore cannot compel enforcement inside Indonesia, so a shared panel is the realistic route to results on both sides.

transcript.position: Indonesia comes to this table to stop the haze, and we propose a deal in which Indonesian courts enforce on Indonesian soil, a moratorium that protects peatland with funded support for smallholders, and district-level fire data shared with the ASEAN monitoring system. Singapore's 24-hour PSI passed 300 in 2015, so the problem is real, but the 2002 ASEAN Agreement already sets the right frame: Article 3(1) of that treaty keeps each party's sovereign right to use its own resources, and Article 9 requires us to control open burning. Because those duties bind us as the territorial state, the Indonesian authorities are the ones who must enforce them, and a Singapore statute that extends to conduct outside Singapore under section 4 cannot replace that. Indonesia will therefore not accept foreign jurisdiction over acts on its soil. The cost is concrete: a foreign court ruling on Indonesian land would set a precedent that every concession dispute could be taken abroad.\n\nThe most damaging objection to our proposal is that Indonesian enforcement alone has failed to stop the fires, and that Singapore needs parcel data to hold culprits to account. We answer it in two ways. First, we will share data aggregated by district, which goes beyond the fire and haze data that Article 8(1) already requires us to send to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, while keeping parcel-level records within domestic data law, since unresolved tenure disputes overlap the concession registry and publishing parcels now would name the wrong owners under the presumption in section 8 of the Singapore Act. Second, we will accept a phased moratorium with some exemptions, run by the provinces and the new Peatland Restoration Agency, which is a real step beyond the status quo. In return, we need full donor funding for the transition, because El Nino conditions with a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter mean smallholders face the planting window with no safe alternative to burning, and we will not impose restrictions on them without funded alternatives. Singapore's own Act caps total fines at S$2 million under section 5(5), so the sums Singapore stands to gain by liability are small beside the tens of billions of dollars in regional losses, and money spent on alternatives for farmers prevents more haze than any fine. If Singapore accepts Indonesian courts and full funding, we can move on the data and moratorium terms it cares about most.

transcript.position: We have moved on two issues since last round: we now accept a full donor fund and a moratorium with partial exemptions, and in return we hold firm on full concession maps and a joint ASEAN panel. Indonesia's strongest point is that parcel data could name the wrong owner under the presumption in section 8 of our Act, and that a wrong record could make an innocent smallholder liable. We answer that the maps would go to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System and to the panel, not be published, and the panel, not a Singapore court, would test every record against tenure disputes before any company is named. Our Act's aggregate fine is capped at S$2 million under section 5(5), so a smallholder is not exposed to ruin by this deal, and we propose that the panel's cases target concession holders, with smallholders handled through the funded alternatives Indonesia itself wants.\n\nIndonesia cares most about enforcement staying regional and about funding, so we aim our offer there. Indonesia's strongest point is that wrong parcel records could name the wrong owner under section 8 of our Act, and that a panel would be an outside body ruling on its territory. We answer both. No transition funding without measurable reductions against the 2015 baseline, because money released on trust leaves donors paying again for the same haze.

transcript.position: We are holding our package because it already contains the moves Singapore says it values most, and we add new safeguards to meet its attribution and accountability worries. Singapore's strongest point is that without parcel maps no one can attribute a fire to a company, because section 8 of its Act proves ownership from maps [S2]. We answer that attribution happens in Indonesian courts, which hold the parcel records, and that we will not ask Singapore to trust us blindly. If a fire burns inside a district, the Ministry and the Peatland Restoration Agency will give the Indonesian court the parcel record for that fire, and the court will publish the outcome and report it to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, which already receives fire and haze data under Article 8(1) [S1]. This answers the question of who holds our courts to account, and it avoids releasing the whole registry while tenure disputes overlap it. A full release would also run against our domestic data law, and a wrong entry could name an innocent holder under the section 8 presumption. A joint panel ruling on acts on our soil would cross our red line on foreign jurisdiction, and Article 27 gives no binding tribunal, so its rulings would have no enforcement behind them [S1].\n\nOn the deal, Singapore puts its weight on maps and a strict moratorium, and it has said funding matters less to it. So we offer the strictest moratorium on companies, with no exemptions, run by the Peatland Restoration Agency and provincial administrations, in return for Indonesian courts and a full donor fund that Singapore now says it will back. We also fix a flaw both sides left open: tranches tied to hazardous PSI days could stop money mid-season because of El Nino, which has a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter [Background], and that would punish smallholders who did nothing wrong. Therefore we propose that tranches be measured on hotspot counts in the districts covered, adjusted for El Nino conditions, and that the smallholder alternatives be paid in advance and not suspended mid-season. Section 6 civil claims in Singapore stay open [S2], so Singapore keeps a remedy if our courts fail to act.

key_claims.claim: Indonesian courts with accountability reporting can deliver attribution without releasing the whole parcel registry.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 8(1) already sends fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, so reporting each court outcome and the district hotspot data through that channel adds a check, while [S2] section 6 leaves civil claims open to people in Singapore if Indonesian courts decline to act.

key_claims.claim: Full parcel maps could make an innocent holder liable while tenure disputes overlap the registry.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 8 presumes the owner or occupier of burning land caused the haze and allows ownership to be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government, so a wrong registry entry would name the wrong party.

key_claims.claim: A joint panel adds no real enforcement because the treaty has no binding tribunal.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 provides settlement only by consultation or negotiation with no court or tribunal, so a panel's rulings on Indonesian concessions would carry no treaty backing.

key_claims.claim: Funding tranches must be adjusted for weather so smallholders are not cut off mid-season.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] The ENSO Diagnostic Discussion of 13 August 2015 gives a greater than 90% chance that El Nino lasts through the 2015-16 northern winter, so PSI days alone could fall short for reasons unrelated to compliance.

concessions: If Singapore accepts Indonesian courts and a full donor fund, Indonesia accepts a full moratorium with no exemptions for companies, run by the Peatland Restoration Agency and provincial administrations.
Indonesia will report each fire case outcome from its courts to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre and share district-level data with the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System.
Indonesia accepts tranche payments tied to hotspot reductions against the 2015 baseline, verified by ASEAN monitoring data, with an El Nino adjustment and advance payment of smallholder alternatives.
red_lines: No foreign jurisdiction over acts on Indonesian soil: a panel or foreign court ruling on Indonesian concessions would set a precedent for every future land dispute.
No restriction that falls on smallholders without funded alternatives: the planting window under El Nino conditions leaves them no safe option otherwise.

scores.justification: A joint panel and a donor fund tied to hotspot and PSI reductions are workable ideas. But the package needs Indonesia to hand over full concession maps, which it has refused. Singapore also does not say who sits on the panel, whether its rulings bind anyone, or who pays into the donor fund.

It cites precise statute figures (S$100,000 per day, section 4, section 5(2)(a)). The package is stated clearly, and the funding is tied to measured reductions in hotspots and hazardous PSI days. It gives no panel powers, no fund size, no reduction thresholds and no moratorium timetable.

It calls dropping direct application of the Act 'a real concession'. It also admits it 'cannot compel enforcement inside Indonesia'. It does not admit the costs of full maps and a no-exemption moratorium for Indonesia, such as the risk of wrongly named owners and the burden on smallholders. It treats sovereignty as an objection to rebut, not a cost it imposes.

The package matches its opening statements, and its offers (phasing the moratorium, the fund tied to results) are framed as conditional. One tension: it calls the Act a 'credible fallback' that gives Indonesia a reason to accept the panel, while also giving up direct application of the Act.

It takes on Indonesia's sovereignty objection directly with Article 3(1) and Article 8(1). It does not address the tenure-dispute and wrong-owner concern or smallholder livelihoods, and it was written before Indonesia's argument, so it only anticipates the opponent.

judgments.summary: Singapore proposes that Indonesia give full concession maps to the regional monitoring system. A joint ASEAN panel would review who is responsible for fires, and Singapore would not apply its own Act directly. It also asks for a full peatland moratorium with no exemptions and a partial donor fund released only against measured falls in hotspots and bad-haze days. The argument rests well on the treaty and Act texts and has clear red lines. It is vague on how the panel would work and how it would be funded, and it does not weigh the costs to Indonesia.
unsupported_claims: Sharing maps with a regional body is 'the means of meeting' the Article 3(1) duty. This is an interpretation, and Article 3(1) does not mention maps.
Without maps 'our law cannot link a fire to a landholder'. Section 8 allows maps from a foreign government but does not make them the only way to prove ownership.

scores.justification: Provincial administration and the Peatland Restoration Agency, plus district-level data, can be done. Full donor funding is a large ask with no named donors, and the argument does not explain how Indonesian courts would deal with companies. Its own admission that Indonesian enforcement alone has not stopped the fires weakens the case.

It names district-level data, a phased moratorium with some exemptions, and the agencies that would run it. It gives no fund amount, no list of exemptions, no phase dates and no reporting interval for the data.

It admits that Indonesian enforcement alone has failed to stop the fires, and that its data offer goes only slightly beyond the existing duty. It admits the moratorium is only a partial step. It does not say what Singapore loses from having no attribution route, beyond restating the objection, or what the donors must pay.

Its package matches its opening framing of Indonesian courts on Indonesian soil, district-level data and a funded transition. Its concessions are explicitly conditional on funding and enforcement terms.

It engages section 4, section 5(5) and section 8 of Singapore's Act. It uses section 8 to argue that parcel maps could name the wrong owner. It also answers the 'most damaging objection' that Singapore needs parcel data. It does not address Singapore's argument that a panel is a regional, not foreign, forum.

judgments.summary: Indonesia proposes that Indonesian courts handle enforcement on Indonesian soil. It would share fire data aggregated by district with the regional monitoring system, but not parcel-level maps. It offers a phased moratorium with some exemptions, run by the provinces and the Peatland Restoration Agency, on condition that donors fully fund the transition. The argument links its refusal to share maps to the risk of wrongly naming owners and ties the funding request to the coming dry season. Several of its supporting facts are not in the scenario or sources, and it does not say how much funding it needs.

Unresolved tenure disputes overlap the concession registry. No source or scenario text supports this.
Money spent on alternatives for farmers prevents more haze than any fine. No source supports this.
Comparing the S$2 million cap with regional losses of tens of billions: section 5(5) caps only the criminal fines, not civil claims under section 6, so the comparison is incomplete.

Neither side says who the donors would be, or how much they would pay and on what conditions. Both a partial fund and a full fund put a cost on third parties that nobody has weighed.
If maps stay withheld or only district-level, nobody explains how any panel or court could attribute a fire to a specific company.
Neither side explains how panel rulings would be enforced when Article 27 provides no binding mechanism.
Neither side says how smallholders would be protected from the burden of a full moratorium, or how companies and smallholders would be treated differently.
Neither side says how reductions would be measured and verified, including baselines and who certifies them, though both rely on this for funding.

Gives a named baseline (2015), a certifier (ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, satellite data), tranche release, and a moratorium exemption limited to existing smallholder plots with a phase-out. It gives no fund size, tranche thresholds or panel composition.

It says openly that section 6 civil claims stay available whatever the panel decides, so Indonesia can price the deal. It also admits that dropping direct application of the Act is a concession. It does not admit that full parcel maps carry sovereignty and wrongful-naming costs beyond saying they would not be published.

It explicitly flags its moves: partial exemptions and a full donor fund instead of a partial one. It holds the maps and panel red lines. The shift from partial to full fund conflicts slightly with its round 1 no-funding-without-results line, but it keeps the tranche condition, so this is explained.

It takes on Indonesia's strongest point, the wrong-owner risk under section 8, and answers that maps go to the panel and not to a Singapore court. It targets Indonesia's priorities of regional enforcement and funding. It does not answer the question of how panel rulings would be enforced.

judgments.summary: Singapore keeps full maps and a joint ASEAN panel as firm requirements. judgments.summary: Indonesia keeps Indonesian courts and district-level data. It now offers a full moratorium for companies and accepts funding released in tranches against measured results from a 2015 baseline, in return for courts-only enforcement and a full donor fund. Whether Indonesian courts have the capacity and independence to investigate concession holders, and what happens if they decline to act.

It does not engage Singapore's argument that district data is too coarse for attributing hotspots, nor Singapore's own move to drop the panel, beyond restating the panel objection.

judgments.summary: Indonesia holds its package: district-level data only, Indonesian courts, a full moratorium on companies, and a full donor fund. Smallholders' livelihoods during the gap before funded alternatives arrive, and how smallholder fires would be counted against the hotspot targets that release money.

transcript.position:
Singapore opens by asking for a settlement that ends the yearly dry-season cycle and can be checked. Between June and October 2015 our 24-hour PSI passed 300 and regional losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars, and no attribution mechanism exists today to tell us which concession caused which fire. Article 27 of the ASEAN Agreement offers only consultation and no tribunal, and Article 8(1) requires only that monitoring data reach the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, so the treaty alone has not stopped a repeat. We therefore propose that Indonesia's ministry responsible for plantations share full concession maps with the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, and that a joint ASEAN panel review attribution and corporate liability. In return, Singapore is prepared to apply our own Act only as a fallback, which respects Indonesia's objection to extraterritorial reach. We would also direct part of our regional development and donor funding to peatland restoration through the new Peatland Restoration Agency, but only against measured reductions in hotspots and PSI days.

The strongest objection to our proposal is that full maps breach Indonesian sovereignty and domestic data law. We answer that the maps would go to a regional ASEAN body, not to Singapore's courts, and that Article 3(1) of the treaty already couples the sovereign right to use resources with a duty not to damage neighbouring states. Without concession-level maps, the ownership proof that Section 8 of our Act allows, and any joint panel too, cannot identify the company responsible. District-level totals would therefore not satisfy us, because they cannot name an owner. If Indonesia accepts full map-sharing and a joint panel, we can accept a partial peatland moratorium with phased exemptions and a donor fund that is only partial, which lowers Indonesia's costs. We will not sign anything without an attribution mechanism, because that would leave our population exposed to a repeat of the 2015 episode with nobody answerable.

key_claims.claim: Attribution needs concession-level maps, because the 2015 episode pushed PSI above 300 and no one could be named as responsible.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] The 24-hour PSI passed 300 between June and October 2015, schools closed, and Indonesia declined to release concession maps to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, so ownership of burning land could not be proved.

key_claims.claim: The existing treaty cannot deliver accountability by itself, so a joint ASEAN panel is a real gain for Indonesia as well as for Singapore.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 limits disputes to consultation or negotiation with no court or tribunal, and Article 8(1) only requires data to flow to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, so a panel adds a mechanism the treaty lacks.

key_claims.claim: Singapore's law can be calibrated and is not a threat to Indonesia's economy, which is why we can accept a joint panel in place of applying it directly.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] Section 5(5) caps the aggregate fine at S$2 million, and Section 8 presumes the landowner caused the haze but relies on maps supplied by a foreign government, so shared maps are what makes the Act workable.

key_claims.claim: Funding will be tied to results because Singapore will not pay for transition without measurable reductions.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] Section 5(2)(a) sets fines at up to S$100,000 per haze day, so a verified reduction in haze days is a measurable benchmark that donors can monitor with the satellite data already available.

concessions: If Indonesia accepts full map-sharing with the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, Singapore will accept a joint ASEAN panel instead of direct application of its Act.
If the attribution mechanism is agreed, Singapore can accept a moratorium with partial exemptions rather than none.
Singapore will back only a partial donor fund, released in tranches against verified reductions in hotspots and PSI days.
red_lines: No settlement without an attribution mechanism: without concession-level data nobody can be named, and Singaporeans would face another PSI above 300 with no recourse.
No transition funding without measurable reductions: unconditional money would reward the 2015 outcome and leave Singapore paying again each dry season.

transcript.position:
Indonesia accepts that the 2015 haze harmed its neighbours and is ready to act, but the fix must run through Indonesian authority and be paid for. Enforcement against fires on our soil stays with Indonesian courts, because the ASEAN Agreement itself keeps each party's sovereign right over its resources in Article 3(1) and settles disputes by consultation in Article 27, with no court or tribunal. Singapore's 2014 Act reaches conduct outside Singapore under section 4, and section 8 presumes that a landholder caused the haze from maps supplied by a foreign government. Applying it here would put foreign courts in judgment over acts on Indonesian territory, which we cannot accept. The Act's own penalties also show that the problem is prevention rather than punishment: the fine is capped at S$2 million in aggregate under section 5(5), so it cannot deter a company, and it does nothing to stop the next fire.

In return for Indonesian-led enforcement, we offer real movement elsewhere. We will give ASEAN's monitoring system concession data aggregated by district, which meets the fire and haze data duty in Article 8(1) while keeping parcel-level records inside Indonesia, as our data law requires and because overlapping tenure claims make raw parcel maps unreliable in court. We will also run a peatland moratorium with some exemptions, through provincial administrations and the new Peatland Restoration Agency. The exemptions are needed because a moratorium that lands on smallholders with no alternative income would push them back to clearing by fire. We have changed our package: we now drop full concession maps and accept district-level data, and we accept a full moratorium with no exemptions that Indonesia has just offered, in exchange for one thing, an independent check on who owns burning land. Indonesia's strongest point is that raw parcel maps could wrongly name a firm or smallholder where tenure disputes overlap the registry, and that Section 5(5) caps our Act's aggregate fine at S$2 million. We accept both, so we will not hold maps outside Indonesia and will not apply our Act. However, Indonesia's own answer leaves a gap that neither side has addressed: the ministry that confirms ownership in each fire case is also the body whose licensing is under scrutiny, so a slow, partial or contested confirmation would leave nobody named. Therefore we ask that each per-fire confirmation be sent to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre within a fixed period, which we propose as 14 days and which the parties would settle in the text, and be reviewed by a joint ASEAN panel that is advisory only. The panel would compare the confirmation with satellite hotspot data and refer any gap to Indonesian prosecutors, who alone would prosecute. This keeps judgment on Indonesian soil in Indonesian hands, so it does not cross the red line on foreign jurisdiction, and it gives us the attribution mechanism we cannot sign without.

In return we back the full moratorium and a full donor fund, which together are what Indonesia says it needs for smallholders during an El Nino with a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the northern winter. Because results-based tranches could leave smallholders without income before reductions can be measured, we propose that the first tranche be paid up front through the Peatland Restoration Agency as bridging income, with later tranches released against hotspot reductions on an El Nino adjusted baseline. That baseline would be set from existing satellite data by the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre, with both countries able to challenge it through consultation under Article 27. We cannot release money without measurable reductions, and this design gives Indonesia early cash and gives donors a test. The total cost and the donor list are not in our sources, so they must be established by a costing led by the Peatland Restoration Agency before any pledge. Until a new instrument is in force, the interim channel is the existing Article 8(1) data reporting plus consultation under Article 27, so the next dry season is not left without a mechanism.

Singapore's strongest point is that our own plantations ministry would be the only source of an owner's name, and that the investigated party should not verify itself. We accept that, so we offer that for every fire the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre receives the ministry's confirmation of the registered holder within a fixed period, and may query it and record any tenure dispute it finds. This answers Singapore's attribution red line without parcel maps leaving Indonesia, which matters because our domestic data law restricts parcel-level disclosure and our tenure disputes overlap the concession registry [Background]. Reporting through the Centre also fits the duty to send fire and haze data to it in Article 8(1) [S1].

On the money, Singapore and we now agree on a full donor fund paid in tranches against hotspot reductions on an El Nino adjusted baseline. Our concern is the gap before reductions can be measured, because El Nino has a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the northern winter [Background] and a smallholder with no income will clear by fire, which Article 9 forbids [S1]. If Singapore accepts Indonesian courts and district data with the Centre's verification role, we will negotiate in good faith on non-binding information sharing in the new ASEAN text.

scores.justification: Results-based tranches tied to hotspot and PSI reductions can be carried out. Full concession maps going to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System collide with Indonesia's stated data law, and a joint panel has no basis in the treaty. Article 27 says disputes are settled by consultation, and Singapore does not say how the panel would be created or what authority it would have. Singapore also does not say what it would pay.

It names the recipient body (the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System), the fallback use of its Act, and funding released in tranches against verified reductions. It gives no amounts, no hotspot or PSI thresholds, no timeline and no panel composition.

It admits that full maps raise Indonesia's sovereignty and data-law objection and says a partial fund and partial exemptions would 'lower Indonesia's costs'. It does not weigh the cost to smallholders or the commercial sensitivity of parcel-level data.

The text says Singapore can accept a partial moratorium with phased exemptions. The proposed package nonetheless specifies a full moratorium with no exemptions. The text also says the Act is a fallback only, while the package lists a joint panel. This conflict is not explained as a negotiating tier, so it reads as an unexplained mismatch.

It confronts the sovereignty and data-law objection directly. It answers with Article 3(1), says the maps go to a regional body and not to Singapore's courts, and explains why district totals 'cannot name an owner'. It also gives up direct application of the Act. It does not engage Indonesia's El Nino or smallholder concern.

judgments.summary: Singapore asks for full concession maps to go to the regional haze monitoring body and for a joint ASEAN panel to review attribution and liability. Its own Act would be a fallback only. It offers partial donor funding released against measured falls in hotspots and haze days. It says it would accept phased moratorium exemptions if the maps are shared. Its stated package asks for a full moratorium with no exemptions, which contradicts that offer. Its supporting evidence is thin on the funding benchmark.
unsupported_claims: Satellite data 'already available' to monitor haze-day reductions is not in any listed source; [S2] s5(2)(a) is a fine provision and says nothing about monitoring benchmarks.
The ministry responsible for plantations is named as the holder of the maps; no source says this.
Singapore would 'direct part of our regional development and donor funding' to the Peatland Restoration Agency; the scenario does not support this, and the Agency is dated to January 2016.
The claim that its law 'is not a threat to Indonesia's economy' rests on the S$2 million cap, which does not show economic impact.

scores.justification: District-level data and a moratorium with exemptions run through provincial administrations and the Peatland Restoration Agency are within its power. The demand for a full donor fund depends on donors Indonesia cannot compel and who have not been identified. Indonesian courts being the only enforcement route is feasible only if they act credibly, which is not shown.

It ties each concession to a condition: district data if Indonesian courts keep enforcement, and partial exemptions if the fund is full. It names the delivery bodies. It gives no fund size, no exemption categories, no phase-in dates and no reporting intervals.

It admits the 2015 haze harmed its neighbours and that smallholders would bear the cost of a ban. It does not admit that district aggregates cannot identify a responsible owner. It also does not admit that Indonesian-only enforcement leaves Singapore with no independent check.

Round 1 is coherent with its own package: district maps, Indonesian courts, partial exemptions and a full fund. The flexibility is conditional and explained: 'If donors fund the transition fully, we can be flexible'. The wording shifts between 'some exemptions' and 'only partial exemptions', which is a small blur.

It answers Singapore's Act directly, citing sections 4, 5(5) and 8. It argues that the S$2 million cap shows the Act cannot deter. It does not answer why district data would meet Singapore's attribution need. It does not engage the idea of a joint panel except through the treaty argument.

judgments.summary: Indonesia says enforcement must stay with Indonesian courts and rejects applying Singapore's Act to Indonesian land. It would give ASEAN's monitoring system concession data aggregated by district. It would run a moratorium with some exemptions through provincial bodies and the Peatland Restoration Agency, and it asks donors to fund the transition in full. It ties further flexibility on exemptions to full funding. It gives few figures. It is weak on the cost to Singapore of having no way to name an owner.
unsupported_claims: El Nino with a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter, cited to an 'ENSO Diagnostic Discussion, 13 August 2015', is not in the scenario or the listed sources.
Overlapping tenure claims make raw parcel maps unreliable in court; no source supports this.
Article 8(1) is stretched: it covers fire and haze data sent by monitoring centres and does not address concession data, so it does not show that district aggregates satisfy the treaty.

The Act 'does nothing to stop the next fire' and 'cannot deter a company' are inferences from the S$2 million cap, not facts in the source. The source also lists a per-day fine of up to S$100,000 under s5(2)(a).
The 'new' Peatland Restoration Agency was established in January 2016, so it did not exist during the 2015 episode.

unaddressed_tradeoffs: Haze depends heavily on weather and El Nino, so results-based funding tied to hotspot or PSI reductions could penalise Indonesia for dry-season conditions outside its control. Neither side proposes a baseline or a weather adjustment.
Neither side says who the donors are, how large the fund would be, or who would pay if donors beyond Singapore do not contribute.
The legal basis and authority of a joint ASEAN panel are not addressed. A panel would need a new instrument, since Article 27 provides only consultation, and its decisions might not bind companies.
Neither side addresses the capacity and independence of Indonesian courts to prosecute powerful plantation companies, or what happens if they do not act.

Companies and smallholders are not at the table. Neither side addresses how plantation firms with overlapping tenure claims would be treated or how commercially sensitive concession data would be protected once it reaches a regional body.
Neither side addresses spillover to other ASEAN members, such as Malaysia, or the precedent a map-sharing or panel deal would set for them.

scores.justification: Offers safeguards (maps go only to the ASEAN body and panel, tenure disputes flagged) and admits a new ASEAN instrument is needed. But the panel needs Indonesian consent, which Indonesia has refused, and no funding amounts or donors are named.

Gives concrete design points: tranches against hotspot counts, an El Nino-adjusted baseline, referral to Indonesian prosecutors, and maps restricted to the monitoring body. It gives no fund size, tranche schedule, baseline method or panel membership.

Concedes the Act is a poor deterrent, that a new instrument is needed, and that El Nino could unfairly penalise Indonesia. It still says little about what full maps cost Indonesia beyond the data-law safeguards.

It flags the change to a partial-exemption moratorium and a full donor fund, and ties both to map-sharing. This matches the round 1 offer to soften if maps are shared. Round 1 proposed no exemptions in its package but said it could accept partial ones, so the 'fixes the contradiction' framing is fair. Red lines are unchanged.

Names Indonesia's strongest point (the S$2m cap and extraterritorial reach), agrees with it, and answers with referral to Indonesian courts. It also addresses data-law and tenure-overlap concerns and the fairness of results-based money.

judgments.summary: Singapore moves toward Indonesia: it drops direct application of its Act, accepts a full donor fund paid in tranches, and accepts a moratorium with partial exemptions. It holds firm on full concession maps going to the ASEAN monitoring body, with safeguards, and on a joint panel that refers findings to Indonesian prosecutors. Its offer answers Indonesia's concerns well. Its main weakness is that the panel and the maps are the points Indonesia has most clearly rejected, and it gives no figures for the fund.
unsupported_claims: Section 5(2)(a) / Article 9 are cited as evidence that the full donor fund is affordable or that prevention of fire clearing is 'the measurable outcome'; neither source addresses fund affordability.
Claim that district totals 'cannot satisfy the treaty's purpose of accountability' goes beyond Article 8(1), which says nothing about accountability or ownership.
Malaysia joining the arrangement and spreading the funding burden has no support in the scenario or sources.

scores.justification: Case-by-case confirmation of the registered holder by the plantations ministry is workable inside Indonesia's existing registry. But a full no-exemption ban in an El Nino year, paid for entirely by donors, is a hard package, and Singapore has not shown it will pay without conditions.

The new channel is concrete: confirm the registered holder per fire to prosecutors and report the outcome to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre. It also names a weather-adjusted baseline and the Peatland Restoration Agency. It gives no response time, no cost figure and no tranche design.

Admits that a full ban hurts smallholders and that the exemptions must return if funding falls short. It gives little on what district-only data and Indonesian-only enforcement cost Singapore, and the 'drop the panel' demand is stated as a trade rather than a cost.

It flags the shift to a full moratorium and says it is conditional on full funding, which follows its round 1 line that full funding makes it flexible. Red lines on foreign jurisdiction and on unfunded smallholder restrictions are unchanged.

Takes up Singapore's point that district totals cannot name a company and offers the per-fire confirmation. It gives the concession Singapore asked for on the moratorium. It does not engage Singapore's safeguards for the maps or its offer to refer panel findings to Indonesian prosecutors, and calls the panel 'binding' though Singapore's panel only refers findings.

judgments.summary: Indonesia concedes a full moratorium with no exemptions, on condition of a fully funded transition. It adds a channel under which its plantations ministry confirms the registered holder of burning land for each fire, reported to ASEAN. It still rejects full maps, a joint panel and application of Singapore's Act. The new channel is a real attempt to meet Singapore's need to name an owner. However, it leaves Indonesia as the only source of attribution and does not engage Singapore's safeguards or its non-binding referral model.
unsupported_claims: Indonesian courts can 'order prosecution and licence action' as a deterrent; no source supports this.
Claim that the S$2 million penalty is 'small against plantation revenues' has no figure for plantation revenues in the scenario or sources.

Overlapping tenure disputes and commercially sensitive data are cited to [Background], but the background gives only Indonesia's reference to sovereignty and domestic data law; the overlap itself is not in the scenario text.
Claim that Singapore's ownership confirmation fits Article 8(1) is a stretch: that article covers fire and haze data, not ownership confirmation.

unaddressed_tradeoffs: Who verifies Indonesia's own per-fire ownership confirmations, and what happens if they are slow, incomplete or contested? Neither side deals with the conflict of interest in having the investigated party confirm ownership.
A full-fund tranche system that is tied to results may leave smallholders without income during the months before any reductions can be measured, so the bridging finance is unaddressed.
Who the donors are, what the full fund would cost, and whether Singapore's payment can be made without a binding ASEAN or donor commitment. Neither names an amount.
A full no-exemption ban could be hard to enforce on smallholders in the 2015-16 dry season, and Indonesia's capacity for monitoring and fire response is not discussed.
What happens if the baseline adjusted for El Nino is disputed, and who sets it.
What happens in the interim, before any new ASEAN instrument is in force, if no panel or data channel exists in the next fire season.

scores.justification: Builds on existing duties: a 14-day report to the Co-ordinating Centre under Article 8(1), consultation under Article 27 as an interim channel, and an advisory-only panel. It admits the cost and donor list are unknown and asks for a costing led by the Peatland Restoration Agency. The new panel still needs a new instrument.

Gives a 14-day deadline, an up-front first tranche paid through the Peatland Restoration Agency, an El Nino adjusted baseline set by the Centre from satellite data, and a challenge route through Article 27. Total cost and tranche sizes are left open.

Concedes maps and application of the Act, and accepts a full moratorium and a full fund. It admits results-based tranches could leave smallholders without income, and that cost and donors are unknown. It says less about the burden an external review places on Indonesia's ministry.

It drops full concession maps and accepts district data, reversing its previous 'district totals cannot satisfy us'. It explains this as a concession to Indonesia's point about overlapping tenure. It keeps the panel and the funding conditions. It now accepts the full moratorium, a move from last round's partial exemptions, explained as taking up Indonesia's offer. The shift on maps is large, and the claim that the attribution need is still met rests on the confirmation channel.

Takes up Indonesia's per-fire confirmation channel, names the conflict of interest in it, accepts the S$2 million cap point and the tenure-overlap point, and adopts the bridging-tranche idea for smallholders. It was written before Indonesia's round-3 argument, so it responds to Indonesia's previous-round offer.

judgments.summary: Singapore gives up full maps and the application of its Act, accepts district data and a full moratorium without exemptions, and builds on Indonesia's own per-fire ownership confirmation. It reverses last round's full moratorium with no exemptions and returns to partial exemptions, explained as an exchange for the up-front tranche.
